utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I would apologise for everybody that we were late in starting because the computer system is giving difficulties. As you may be aware, it is still not fully functioning and we hope we can manage to continue while the technical people are attempting to correct the problem. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon everybody and we will continue with the testimony of the witness, and this witness is a protective-measures witness, so to say. I would like when we start to be in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the morning of the 20th, between 6.00 and 7.00, an order came through for all of us who were in the hospital explicitly for those slightly wounded and all the others to leave the hospital building. There was panic among the people. We started leaving the building. At the exit, there were a lot of soldiers and Major Sljivancanin was among them. At the door, there was a soldier whose name was Nikola Dukic --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Tuma, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why is that necessary for private session, Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In order, while she is defining, mentioning names, it could be in the long run to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It depends whose name it is and is there a problem with this soldier?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The soldier is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would not think there is justification for private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This soldier stood at the exit separating men from women. Men were leaving on one side, that was to the left as you enter the hospital, and the women went to the right. At this same exit, I did not know where to go. I just stopped right there. I was standing a few feet behind Major Sljivancanin. My husband was led away. There were buses waiting for them already. He got on to one of those buses and that was -- that was the last I saw of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the morning, you were mentioning at 6.00 to 7.00, where were you in the morning when this order came where you were told to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were perhaps about a dozen of us sleeping in a room. We were lying on the ground. There were mattresses that we were using and we slept there. Then the order came so we packed in a rush, not that we had many things to pack anyway, a few personal belongings, and then we left the hospital, or, rather, the hospital building. We passed through a long corridor. It was some sort of a basement, not quite underground but some sort of a basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here that the order came that you should pack. In what way? Who gave that order to you and the rest of the people who were in that room on the mattresses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers were out in the corridor and they were telling people to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers in JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there anyone you could recognise amongst those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the hospital itself, but outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are just talking about in the morning when the order came, so -- and then you mentioned that you saw a soldier came, soldiers came. And my question is if you could recognise any of those soldiers who gave the orders that you should pack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those who entered the building to tell us that we should get out, I did not recognise any of those, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from whom the order came from? Who ordered to pack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite clear that Major Sljivancanin was in charge and giving orders. He was giving all the orders and they were obeying him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of this specific order that you should pack and leave the hospital, was he the one who gave that order? Were you in that impression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression, yes. I didn't hear him from him directly, but who else could have given that order if it hadn't been him who was standing outside the hospital? He was the one that people went to for instructions because he was the one who was there in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him around in the morning when this specific event took place, when you were told to pack and to leave the hospital? Just in the beginning of the morning, just on that phase of the day, so to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very exit of the building, there was Major Sljivancanin. He was talking to a man in white, most probably someone from one of the international missions. I don't speak English but I speak Croatian. That man demanded that a list be made with all the people who were being taken away and boarded on to buses. However, this gentleman did not authorise that and I quote, I think this is exactly what he told him. He said, "Sir, listen, this country belongs to me and I am the one giving orders here. When I come to your country I will submit myself to whatever you say." And he refused to allow for those people to be listed. That is why those people were taken away without previously being recorded on lists. They were taken to those buses, including my husband who is still missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard it with my own ears. I was standing three feet perhaps behind Major Sljivancanin, behind his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this particular event, did Sljivancanin introduce him in a specific way? Did you hear anything about that, to the man in white?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said his name was Major Sljivancanin. He did say that. I wouldn't have known that it was him if I hadn't heard it from him that very morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he in that sense say anything about his own position above that he was a major and positioned in the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this man who wanted to have a list drawn up with all the wounded, he was adamant about this, and then he told him what he told him. He introduced himself saying he was Major Sljivancanin, that this was his country, and that he was in charge here and, well, nothing; they just talked on. The other man was speaking in English and I didn't understand what he was saying but I'm telling you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just quote you here. You said that he was -- that he told that he was in charge here. What is your impression about what he was meaning by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he was the one determining what would happen to those people who were being taken away. Determining what would become of us who were still there. The entire hospital, all the people inside the hospital. He was the one determining what would happen to everyone. Nobody was free to leave or go wherever they wanted. It all had to be done the way that he had ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in no position to interrupt. This whole line of questioning, there are two things that I believe to constitute drawbacks. A, the questions are leading. B, the witness is asked to speculate and to assume what the role of Mr. Sljivancanin might have been. This calls for speculation and this speculation is obtained by a series of extremely leading questions. There were several such questions. For example, on page 5, line 25, and several other questions. I hoped that this would soon stop but now I see that the whole set of questions is very leading and I don't think questions of this sort should be asked on examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your reference to line 25, Mr. Lukic, I don't see that to be a leading question. There had been, though, some other questions that were, and I think the proposition basically put by Mr. Lukic, Mrs. Tuma, is sound. You can get from this witness what she saw, what she heard, what people were doing. But then trying to have her add to that by saying what her impression was of what somebody meant or so forth is just pushing too far. The facts will speak for themselves as to what she saw and what she heard. So if you would keep it down to her observations, sight and sound, the events that were actually occurring, I think we'll avoid the problems that Mr. Lukic has drawn attention to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In that -- in the hospital, during that morning, and now we are -- I'm talking about Wednesday, the 29th [sic] of November 1991, did you see in the morning in the hospital or at any time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's recorded as 29 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I said 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just so it's clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: November the 20th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any kind of selection of people inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th, as I was passing down that corridor, there was a doctor, I'm not quite sure which one it was but I believe it was Dr. Stanojevic. He was there with a high military official whose rank I didn't know because I don't know about these things. He spoke to him, however, saying, "Comrade Mrksic." They were walking together down that corridor, and this doctor who, by the way, hails from Vukovar and he knew most of the patients, was saying this one is ours and this one isn't. This is one of us, and this one isn't, meaning this one is a Serb and the one who wasn't one of theirs was a Croat. This is what I heard when I was walking down that corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you heard this, what was your distance to this -- the people that were walking, when you overheard they said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a few feet away but there were wounded lying on either side of the corridor in beds. Those were seriously wounded persons who couldn't just get up and leave the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear clearly what was saying -- what was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it loud and clear when he spoke to him saying, "Comrade Mrksic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened directly after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, we were standing outside and this one soldier - I can't say which one because I didn't know them - said to separate the Serbs from the Croats. There was a separation of Serbs and Croats because both Serbs and Croats were in the hospital as well as a number of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at this point of time standing outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still standing where I was, once I had got out. We had to wait there for further orders that would tell us where to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the entrance of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the wounded were leaving the building, I was there and a man in uniform came up and talked to a lady. She asked what would become of them and he said, "They will all be killed. This is something that's been agreed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they then talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were talking about the people who had been taken aside and taken to the buses early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are referring to the people, can you more -- be more specific about that? Who that group, who they comprised of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were slightly wounded, and the staff, medical staff, help workers, all those who were able to move. Those who were in the hospital when they were being separated, when men were being taken to one side and women to the other. That's when they went to the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned here that men were taken to one side and the others to -- and women to the other. At that -- did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that. I experienced that. I had been separated from my husband. We left the hospital building together and then we were separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were separated from your husband, were there any kind of soldier present at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a soldier who separated us, so, yes, there were soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of soldier or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing JNA uniforms or some other sort of uniform but I don't think so because they were there with the JNA. So I don't know. They were wearing a uniform, military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any kind of directions giving at -- at this event by any soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was that one standing at the door, sending men to one side and women to the other, separating them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there anyone overseeing what happened at this specific incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was standing there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was standing there. Did he do anything? Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't really listening because he was talking to his soldiers. I was standing in a group of people where the women were and we were waiting to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your impression of -- in how he was in the way he was acting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, same question. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting to hear how the question was understood by the witness. It may be satisfactory. It may go over the edge. So I'm alert to your problem, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I will repeat exactly what I said through reading the transcript. What is your impression of -- in how he was in the way he was acting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression, there was no impression. There was just a lot of fear. He was acting in a soldierly kind of way. He was being strict, but that was the approach that he took probably because he was a professional soldier. I can only tell you that I was certainly very scared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you scared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had been in the basement for a full three months. We were being shelled, day in, day out, and then they started separating us, men to one side and women to the other. What else could I have felt but fear? I felt fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fear of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fear that we would perhaps all be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened exactly after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was still standing there, they carried another wounded person out on a stretcher, the soldiers did, they dropped him from the stretcher and started kicking him. I don't know what happened to that wounded person later. This was perhaps ten metres away from where I was standing myself. Later on, we were ordered to leave the hospital courtyard. Again there were buses waiting there that we, the elderly, women and children, were supposed to board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here that they carried a wounded -- another wounded person out on stretchers. Who were -- who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally knew that wounded person who was there. He had a plaster cast on all the way up to his hip. His name was Martin Dosen. I knew the man and I saw them drop him off the stretcher and kick him, but that was all I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see later on or exactly after that what happened with this specific person, Dosen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. I left the hospital perimeter and then we were standing by the road side for a long time waiting for those buses to take us somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who kicked him, Dosen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers kicked him, soldiers in uniform. I'm not sure which uniform, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there more than one who kicked him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four of them carrying the stretcher. I only saw what I've just told you. There were four of them carrying the stretcher and then they chucked him from the stretcher and started kicking him on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this take -- where did it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened near the hospital exit, between the hospital exit and the buses waiting midway down the road. I don't think the distance is greater than 20 metres. 20 metres, tops. From the hospital exit to where the buses were, midway down that path or road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where the men went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that either because I was already on the other side of the hospital, or, rather, I was already in another street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened to you? You were standing you said here on the other street. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we stood there, a lot of soldiers passed by. They walked in groups, carrying a horrible-looking flag with skulls. They also sang a song that went something, "Slobodan get some salad. There will be meat because we will be slaughtering Croats." As for us, we stood in a line waiting to board the buses which were supposed to take us somewhere but at that time we still didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were standing there waiting, did you observe anything that you -- that could be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a lot of soldiers. Then finally, the buses arrived at about 11.00 or 11.30, I don't know, I'm not sure, and then we boarded the buses and they drove us away. Those were green military buses, not civilian buses, the buses belonging to the army, JNA. Then they drove us through the town. There were bodies all strewn around through the town, bodies of dead people, and then we went through Ralik and some villages and arrived in Sremska Mitrovica that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you were entering the buses, did you see any other civilians around you except for that group that yourself were part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were very many civilians, women, children, the elderly, there were a lot of us. There were several buses there that took us away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other people than the people that were later on taken away in the buses when you were standing outside waiting for the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw the soldiers singing the songs. They stood in groups. They arrived in groups carrying flags with them and singing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any people that were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think there were any such people in our bus, not in the bus where I was. I don't think that there were any wounded persons there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking about the people in the bus. I'm asking about when you were standing outside waiting to entering the buses, when you were waiting for the buses, if you were at that point see any injured people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were wounded people there. The ones who had been separated, who used to be in the hospital and then were separated from us. There were a lot of wounded people there, slightly wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people that were wounded or injured than the ones you have already said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think I saw any.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the permit answer of the court, if that is allowed, to show the witness her statement given to the OTP investigator on the 18th July, 1992, in order to ask her or remind her what she then said to the investigator when she was questioned at that time concerning this specific question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You propose to see that the witness see the statement to see whether it refreshes her memory, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection -- is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honours. First of all, I think that this must be a 1995 statement and I believe that this must be just a typo. But I also have an objection to this type of approach in refreshing the witness's memory. You can see that the OTP has already talked to this witness and they have shown the statement to the witness and this was done as recently as several days ago. I don't think that this is an appropriate way to conduct chief examination. Questions put in chief examination should be such so that the witness is able to answer questions on their own, without any further guidance. This witness was shown the statement several days ago and now her memory needs to be refreshed once again. We received corrections which means that they talked to this witness as recently as several days ago, so this statement must have been shown to the witness in order to make corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal, in keeping with the jurisprudence of many nations that have an adversarial system, does allow in these circumstances that the witness may refresh her memory from a statement previously made. I would make it clear that the position varies between some adversarial countries. In my own country, this would not be allowed. But it is the position in many and it is the established jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Chamber, though, well knows at what point the witness was asked to refresh her memory and, of course, that will be taken into account in assessing what weight we might ultimately attach to evidence that comes only because it's been refreshed. The witness may see the statement, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, which statement it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. It is the statement taken on the 18th July, 1995, by the investigator who was representing the Office of the Prosecutor, Jose Limmayog Jr. And that statement is also signed by the current witness. And also, the part that I would like specifically to show the witness is on page 4 in the English version and also the same page, number 4, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness should be directed to the page and the particular part, asked to read it, and then, with the statement put aside, you may ask her whether she remembers certain matters, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the information of the Court, that I don't know the B/C/S language. I can -- yeah. It should be this specific part in the B/C/S but I'm not 100 per cent sure while my language skills, not yet at least, entails also B/C/S language. But I can -- I can show her the part that I most certainly think is the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How will Defence counsel no what part it is that you are referring the witness to? Have you got a copy that can be passed over in the B/C/S that marks the passage?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it here. I will now show the usher which part I'm meaning. Starting here -- it's starting there and it's ending -- it's just two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Has that been shown to Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can I do that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The usher will pass it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has now seen the passage? And your question, Mrs. Tuma? Non-leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- I'm asking the witness, did you see any other injured persons when you were standing outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got mixed up. I mixed up those days to some extent. But at any rate, when they took away this slightly wounded persons, there were hospital workers among them, drivers, help workers, and so on. To -- I don't know where they took them. Most likely to Velepromet, but I don't know that for a fact. Then they asked Major Sljivancanin to bring back the people who had hospital IDs on their pockets, proving that these people were hospital staff, that they worked at the hospital. Once those people were brought back, we were still there and those people were brought back with bloody faces and they were beaten in a place that they had been taken to. So these are the people that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the gender of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of them were never found, Jozo Adzaga and Jozo Zeljko. They were in the group that was returned but it seems that after that, they were taken some place again and now they are missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No more questions, please. I'm done with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tuma. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic will now have some questions for you. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I need a moment to get ready. I need to take the lectern because I wasn't expecting the examination in chief to be concluded so soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. Let me introduce myself. I'm attorney-at-law Miroslav Vasic. In view of the fact that you're a protected witness I would kindly ask you to make a pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters can interpret what you say and what I say and so that your voice would not be heard through my microphone; therefore, I need enough time to switch off my microphone. In addition, I would like to ask you to answer my questions with a yes or a no, unless my question is such that it requires a longer answer. In view of everything you have told us here in the previous day and a half, it seems that you are quite bitter about all of the Serb nationals who took part in the events and that you refer to them as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't refer to them as Chetniks. I referred to them as members of the army. As for me being bitter, no. I'm not. Rather, I am very sad and unhappy about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any bitter feelings towards the JNA? Do you believe them to be responsible for the tragedy that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a politician and I know nothing about that. I'm a simple civilian who lived in the city of Vukovar. I experienced these events. I lost my whole family and have nobody anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you thus believe that no sentence would be sufficient to ameliorate the pain that you have suffered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What have I have with these sentences? I can't explain to you how I feel. What are those sentences to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we have already heard, in June of 1995, you gave a statement to the OTP representatives, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You waited for 14 years since the events in Vukovar to be invited to come here and to tell everyone what has been bothering you all these years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you gave your statement in July of 1995, you expected to be invited to come to testify in the course of 1998, when a trial was held here against the then accused Slavko Dokmanovic, who was accused precisely for the events that we are discussing here. However, you were not invited to come here and testify.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. In addition to that, I wasn't present in the areas where those events took place and where Slavko Dokmanovic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then disappointed that the Prosecution failed to invite you to come and testify about the events you described in your statement, given in July of 1995, thus never giving you a chance to come to the Court and describe your experiences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected them to invite me to come here but I wasn't surprised at not being invited at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, did you come here now wishing to ensure, through your testimony, that these accused would receive the longest possible sentences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the time being, nothing has been proven yet. Once it's proven, the Court will decide. As for my wishes, I have none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after 14 years, you have an opportunity to testify before the Trial Chamber. Do you believe that you have a right to represent certain details or events in the light that you wish to attribute to them even though you yourself didn't see or hear these details or events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right. I would never describe something of the sort, even though it's been 14 years, 1991 is as fresh in my mind as it was back then. It will remain that way until I die. When I close my eyes, I can see and hear everything that happened back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it or hear it even better in 1995 when you gave your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back then, I gave the same statement. I only can describe one version. There is only one statement I can give, and that is the one describing what I experienced and saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony, Defence received from the OTP corrections to your 1995 statement. Were these corrections written on the basis of what you discussed with them in the past 10 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been very many years. It's been a lot of years. And if perhaps one word was amiss, that doesn't mean that you can put these questions to me now. Everything I stated is true, and 1991 was 14 years ago, 1995 was ten years ago, and it is possible that a word can be wrong here or there. But the essence of what I said is always the same, both what I said in 1995 and what I said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I just go back in the transcript here, what the Defence is saying that, it's line 6 or so, yeah, "corrections written on the basis of what you discussed with them in the past 10 days." That could be interpreted as that OTP discussed with the witness during 10 days, and I would like to add that the addendum that has also been disclosed to the Defence was done on the 31st of October, 2005. It was one day and not 10 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Defence doesn't have a problem with that. We didn't really claim that the OTP spent 10 days talking to the witness but that, rather, it was done within the past 10 days. At any rate, thank you, my learned friend from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you please tell us whether your recollections were fresher in 1995 when you gave your statement then or today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are equally fresh when it comes to the 1991 events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about when you first gave your statement to the OTP back in 1995? Did you not state that you would answer truthfully any questions and to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you'd given your statement, once the statement had been typed up, was the statement read back to you in the Croatian language and did you not sign the statement to confirm everything that is in it? Did you not thereby confirm that the statement reflected your recollection of how things happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When making corrections to your statement on the 31st of October, 2005, did you perhaps want to help the OTP through these corrections so that they may be better able to present the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you made these corrections, did perhaps one of my learned friends from the OTP explain that some of the things you stated in your first statement were not quite consistent with some parts of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have forgotten something myself. It's been a long time, after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, but I asked whether my learned friends from the OTP perhaps explained to you during your briefing session that some of the things you had stated in your previous statement were not perhaps consistent with some allegations made in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were making corrections to your 1995 statement, did my learned friends from the OTP show you any other statements by other witnesses who speak differently of the same things that you are speaking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your submission, Madam, that you now remember things more clearly now, 14 years after, than you did in 1995, three and a half years after the facts, when you gave your first statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything like that. There may be minor inconsistencies, a word that slipped through the cracks, something like that, but basically I keep stating the same thing and all I am saying something based on what I saw and heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You took an oath here before this Honourable Trial Chamber. I hope that you are aware of your duty to tell the truth as well as the consequences should you fail to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if this might be a convenient time to break or perhaps I should press on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of the late start, we thought to go to about ten minutes to 4.00, but if it would be of significant advantage to you, we could break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I just thought that I should like to be in keeping with the well-established courtroom schedule. As far as I'm concerned, I'm prepared to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Another 15 minutes or so, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in The Hague, which witnesses were you were touch with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet any of the witnesses at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm staying at a different hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at least you do know that these other witnesses are staying in a different hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the witnesses who came before me were in a different hotel. I'm in a different hotel myself. I'm not here on my own. I'm being accompanied by someone and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your arrival in The Hague, did you meet Dr. Bosanac in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't meet Dr. Bosanac. She was already in The Hague when I was arriving in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival in this courtroom, did you perhaps have an opportunity to follow the testimonies of other witnesses who have appeared in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't watch television much these days, and I don't really follow that particular subject matter. It causes me so much disquiet that I have trouble sleeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your family? Were any of your family members also members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't really tell you about one of my sons. I can't be sure. I know that I myself wasn't. I couldn't say positively about my son but I never saw a membership card or anything. However, I can't fully commit myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who won the local elections in Vukovar back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, the SDP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that election, was Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, a member of the SDP, not elected president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at one point in the summer of 1991, the government of the Republic of Croatia replaced the legally elected president, Slavko Dokmanovic, and appointed in his place a commissioner from their own ranks, the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was never into politics. I just did my job so this wasn't something I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone in your family a member of the ZNG, National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he attended a meeting of the ZNG that was organised in Bogdanovci by Tomislav Mercep in March 1991 where about 2.000 volunteers assembled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. You can go on like this for the whole day asking me questions about this but I still know nothing about it. I know nothing about the political parties, I know nothing about Mercep. I know nothing about this meeting that was purportedly organised. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that as early as May 1991, Croats were organising themselves into groups all over Vukovar in order to defend, as they said, from the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made myself very clear. I'm no politician, and these topics are not part of my testimony or experience. A lot of things happened in Vukovar, many things, all sorts of things. It's just that I can't talk about many things. I don't think that this should be part of my testimony, specifically what happened in May. I really can't testify about that. It would only make things more complicated. I would then remember what happened in Borovo Selo in May. But these are all things that I heard. This would be based on hearsay because I witnessed none of those incidents nor was I directly involved in any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear any of the explosions that resounded all over Vukovar in May, June, and July, when Serb-owned buildings were being blown up as well as kiosks owned by the Borba newspaper company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the barracks is in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the summer of 1991, the barracks was blocked by ZNG members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that sometime later, after the barracks' electricity and water supplies were cut off, as well as their telephone lines, the barracks was subjected to attacks by the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll agree, won't you, that it was only as late as August 1991 that clashes occurred between the ZNG and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in August. I think it was August when fierce shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please go into private session briefly? I have a brief set of questions that might compromise the protective measures granted to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to some questions about the witness's family. So perhaps it would be good to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are hesitant, Mr. Vasic, but, yes, we will go into private for a little while and see whether it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that after the 18th, many people started moving towards the hospital in the belief that the hospital was a safe place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the MUP and the ZNG also came with the civilians to the hospital because they were withdrawing from the frontlines at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that from the 16th of November, the news spread through Vukovar that all those from the hospital would be evacuated under the supervision of the European observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did hear something, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know anyone who was a member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son was, I told you, and his colleagues. There were people like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the colleagues that you mentioned in the hospital after November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ones that I knew went to carry out a breakthrough. The police and the young men from the ZNG went before the hospital -- before the soldiers came to the hospital, to try to break through in the area towards Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about this attempt to break through to Vinkovci? How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. All I know is that they talked when they came to Vinkovci and Zagreb, that they had assembled and then at night they had set out to do that. Some of them were killed there because the terrain was mined. Some of them were swimming across the Vuka river in November. Some of them stayed alive going through the fields, which were mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you that considerable number of members of the ZNG remained in Vukovar who did not participate in this attempt to break through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything like that, no. Many of them were killed, about 5.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this action to break through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in the course of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that some members of the MUP changed into civilian clothes in the hospital in order to leave the hospital with civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the members of the MUP who were securing the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any security at the doors to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go out through the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the period from September until the 20th of November, you never left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That whole time was spent in the cellar, in the -- below ground level. Whoever ventured outside was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any ambulance drivers in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they left the hospital premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a shell fell somewhere and killed and wounded many people, then they had to go and pick up the wounded there and then they brought them to the hospital, so that would be that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those ambulance drivers were alive until November 1991, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were alive. A driver drives a car. But if I ventured outside on the streets, I would probably be struck by a shell or by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you prepare the hospital meals? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one room, that was the ear, nose, and eye department. There was a stove there. It was an improvised area. And that was where we were making the meals because the proper hospital kitchen was damaged with shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the place that you are talking about now was in the basement of the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 18th and the 19th of November, did you prepare meals for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing much to prepare because there was nothing left. There was panic at the time. We were making tea. We had some flour left so we were making some kind of bread or dough. The flour, we mixed it with water and just fried it in oil, so this is what we served.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, breakfast was prepared in the morning for the hospital, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not set. On the 19th and the 20th, there was no breakfast. Nobody had anything to eat. There was no breakfast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that some hospital kitchen staff asserted that on the 17th, 18th, and even the 19th in the morning, they prepared food for the hospital, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say anything, if that is what they said that's fine. But I'm telling you what I'm telling you now because that's what the situation was for a couple of days before that, that we didn't really have anything left in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The witness is asking questions that could perhaps reveal her identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have more questions of this type, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there is no danger since we did hear that there were a lot of people. But I don't have any more questions which would focus on some small group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last few days spent in the Vukovar Hospital, did you move in the rooms where the wounded were staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in a small area that I had to cross in order to reach the toilets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did you hear that some of the wounded were bandaged by the doctors or that the doctors put plaster on them in order to pass them off as the wounded even though they weren't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. I didn't go and mix with the medical staff. I just stayed in the kitchen. No, no. I didn't hear that. I especially didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given on the 18th of July 1995, did you state explicitly to the OTP investigators that in the second part of -- on the day on the 19th of November, you saw Bogdan Dukic, Darko Fot, Mirko Vojnovic, and Marko Savic -- excuse me, Mirko Savic, taking out Martin Dosen who was on a stretcher and that they dumped him into the yard to die there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not how I stated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please give a copy of the B/C/S statement to the witness so that I can ask her to read out the text in paragraph 1 on page 4 of the B/C/S version. This can be found on page 3, paragraph 2, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, would you please read out the first paragraph on page 4 of your statement, slowly, please, to so that the interpreters can interpret that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 19th of November, Vukovar fell. Many civilians kept arriving in the hospital throughout the entire day, seeking shelter. I can't say exactly how many there were. In the second half of the day, the JNA soldiers entered the hospital. Dr. Bosanac negotiated with the members of the JNA to secure the hospital, i.e., to prevent the Chetniks from entering it. JNA promised to us that we would be evacuated to Croatia without problems. However, many Chetniks managed to enter. The hospital had a main entrance and another entrance into the basement. There were also two gates in the hospital yard. The Chetniks, whom I saw enter the hospital with the JNA soldiers, were Bogdan Dukic, Darko Fot. Mirko Vojnovic, nicknamed Capalo, and Mirko Savic. I saw them take out Martin Dosen, who was one of the wounded in the hospital. Although he was on a stretcher, they still pushed him and just dumped him into the courtyard -- in the courtyard, to die. He's among those listed as missing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing the document any longer. Could the usher give it back to me if that's not any problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While giving evidence today, when asked by my learned friend, did you state that you only saw some people beating Martin Dosen but you didn't see other cases of beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement I gave in 1995, all of that is included. It is stated there that I recognised the soldiers because they were from Vukovar. However, I didn't explicitly state that they were the ones carrying Martin Dosen. That was a mistranslation. Martin Dosen was carried on the 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain, then, that in your statement, and you just confirmed to us that this is the statement you gave in 1995, it is stated that you saw that on the 19th? Is your memory fresher today or was it fresher then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollections are quite fresh, and they were so -- and they were just as fresh back then in 1995. People were carried out on the 20th, not on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, you spoke here about the incident involving Martin Dosen, not about the wounded being taken out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin Dosen was seriously injured. He was unable to walk. Therefore he was carried outside of the building on a stretcher and then they dumped him out of the stretcher and started beating him. That's what I saw and that's what I said here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you told us that you didn't see the soldiers beating anyone on the 20th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for Martin. I didn't see other cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you say to us today that you didn't know who beat Martin Dosen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I stated. I stated that in my original statement and, as for the soldiers whose names I gave, those were the soldiers who were in front of the hospital on the 19th afternoon. I recognised them because they were the ones who walked about the premises with rifles in their hands, and all of us recognised them because they were people from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again I have to refer you to your statement given in 1995. You read out the statement to us, rather, a sentence stating that you saw them take out Martin Dosen, who was one of the wounded in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, please make sure you make pauses because of my microphone which is turned on. And then you stated that Bogdan Dukic, Darko Fot, Mirko Vojnovic and Mirko Savic took away Martin Dosen. Please tell me what is the truth here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a case of mistranslation, nothing else. These people were there. Martin Dosen, however, was taken out of the hospital on the 20th in the morning. I've already stated this three times. He was taken out by the soldiers whom I didn't recognise and then these soldiers beat him. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If this is a case of wrong translation, why did you say, then, in your statement that these individuals dumped Martin Dosen out of the stretcher and left him in the yard to die? Was that translated wrongly as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers dumped him, yes. It doesn't platter which soldiers. Some soldiers dumped him. They dumped him out of the stretcher, beat him, and left him there. I don't know what happened with him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given in 1995 to the OTP, did you say that on the 20th of November, in the morning, as you were standing in the yard, you saw many local Chetniks beating men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They searched them, took everything out of their pockets, and as for beating them, well, yes, they would hit them in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, you told us that you didn't see any cases of beating except for Martin Dosen. What is the truth here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is the truth. Everything I said. They didn't really beat them seriously. They simply pushed them. They would take everything out of their pockets and then push them aside in order to pass through. That's what happened. I didn't see anybody's head being broken because that didn't take place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who were there or, as you said that I'm referring to them Chetniks, I have to tell you that we called them Chetniks, those who were in Vukovar because they referred to Croats as Ustashas. So those were Chetniks who were there with the JNA. They were not there on their own. They were there with Major Sljivancanin and with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today that 16 men who had hospital ID badges were boarded on a bus; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These men left together with all other men who had been separated in front of the hospital. Those 16 of them, I am not sure whether there were exactly 16 or perhaps a bit more, or a bit less, had also been separated from the group and put on buses. However, somebody asked -- I'm not sure who did -- some women probably, women who worked at the hospital, asked Mr. Sljivancanin to bring back their husbands, brothers and so on, and after a certain period of time, I wouldn't know exactly how long, these 16 men were brought back. They had been beaten, they were all bloody. They had been beaten somewhere, maybe at Velepromet. You will ask me whether I saw this. No, I didn't see this but all of them said that they had been at Velepromet and were then brought back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to interrupt you because I'm afraid that your voice will be heard through my microphone but I would kindly ask you not to answer in such a detailed manner. So all of these people were brought back because they had hospital ID badges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that in their statements, hospital workers said that all of those people who had hospital ID badges were never boarded on buses, that they were left standing in front of the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. Nobody could have stated anything like that because back then nobody even ever mentioned those hospital ID badges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you standing next to the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The buses were parked in the yard. However, one could see them. They were some 15 to 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know, then, whether somebody asked for their badges or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stood there at the exit. This is where it was decided who would go where. This is where they separated men from women, and this is where men were boarded on buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that upon the return of these buses into the hospital yard, one of the hospital workers had to guarantee that the person on the bus was a colleague hospital worker before that person would be allowed to get off the bus precisely because they didn't have their ID badges on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stand close to the buses upon their return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were still standing there when they came back, all beaten up. The bus parked a bit further away and they walked back and then went to look for their wives or whoever they had there. At any rate, they came back and after a certain period of time, when it was time for us to go to our buses, the buses where the women went to, then the men who had been brought back joined the women and went together to those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't know how did they get off the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them when they came back. I don't understand your question. What do you mean how they got off the buses?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody had to confirm that they were indeed hospital workers? That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said today in answer to a question by my learned friend from the OTP that one of the local Serbs said to a lady that they would all be killed and that this was something that had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this happen? Where did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way out of the hospital building, at the exit, right there. There was a group much women, we were standing there waiting, this uniformed man came along, he was rather senior, grey hair, quite tall. There was this lady who asked him where they were taking the men, and he said quite literally, "They will all be killed. This has been agreed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this lady was that he spoke to? Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know neither of them. The lady was probably a civilian, someone who came to Vukovar in order to escape from elsewhere. Maybe they even knew each other. She took shelter in the hospital. That's what I was trying to say. He came up to her. He talked to her. I was nearby, so naturally I overheard their conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know who this person is? You did say that he was a local Serb after all, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say a local Serb, I apply that only to those I know personally. All the others were all the same thing, all equal to me, they were just military personnel wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that woman, too, a local resident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably she was, since she happened to be in the Vukovar Hospital. I'm sure that she was a local, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you apply the term "local" to a person, you mean you know somebody personally, and yet you used this very term in your 1995 statement to the OTP. You said "a local Serb" and you repeated that in front of this Trial Chamber today. Does that mean that you actually knew this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that person. When I say a local Serb, that means a Serb from Vukovar. That's what I would generally mean by using that term. I didn't know this person. I didn't know him personally. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard what he said, did that scare you? Did that leave a deep impression on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did frighten me for the simple fact that my husband had already been led away. I wanted to go and speak to someone but there was no one for me to speak to. I wanted to plead that they bring him back because he was handicapped. He was disabled. That's what I believed then and I still believe that. He would not have been able to fight actively. I wanted him brought back so that we may leave and, as I was hoping, go back to our homes but this wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This frightened you so much, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Scared you to that extent that you only remember it now, 14 years later; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've known this from day one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why didn't you say so to the OTP in July 1995, if indeed you've known this from day one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had to tell the whole story of what happened in Vukovar in 1991, I wouldn't be out of this courtroom for the next three years. I can't say everything. I can't say the whole story, and I can't necessarily remember all the things at any one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did say that your apprehension actually had to do with your father [as interpreted]. Was that not material in 1995 when you first told the story?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was relevant then as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 46, line 9, there is a mistake in the transcript. Instead of father it should read "husband".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you will agree with me when I say that you never in fact mentioned this prior to 2005, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that this man said what he said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't occur to me. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that when you were in the hospital corridor, you heard a doctor speaking to an officer addressing him as "Comrade Mrksic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was with you, if anyone, when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband and I were walking down that corridor where the wounded were lying and we were carrying a bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that doctor for us, please? The doctor who, as you say, said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a white coat on, middle aged, and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stanojevic, I think. I'm not sure that's 100 per cent correct, but I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the officer now, please, the officer that the doctor spoke to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. He was wearing a uniform, and the two of them were walking down that corridor. There were beds on either side with wounded persons in them. The doctor was saying, "This one is ours and this is not one of ours." That's what I heard. That's what I witnessed. I just walked by, of course, I didn't stop to listen to their conversation. I just walked by and left the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of uniform was that officer wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they all wore the same kind. They were all wearing JNA uniforms. It's not like the Serbs had their own special uniform in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage but I can remember the colours. It's been 15 years. It's very difficult to talk about the colours of their uniforms. He was certainly wearing a uniform and not civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, but 15 years later, you happen to remember that there was a doctor who addressed a military officer by saying, "Comrade Mrksic." That's why 15 years later I think it's perfectly reasonable to ask you. This "Comrade Mrksic," what sort of uniform was he wearing? Do you think you can answer that or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably a military uniform. What other kind of uniform could it possibly have been?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you absolutely positive that you remember correctly what you have just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember their conversation. I was passing by and I heard him say, "Comrade Mrksic." But that's all I know and I said so at the outset. I just walked past them and left the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning when we were on our way out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was between 6.30 and 7.00. I couldn't be more specific because I wasn't wearing a watch. I know it was early in the morning when we were supposed to leave the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that you remember this event clearly, but isn't this the first time you've ever mentioned it? Isn't it true that this is the very first time that you have referred to it? You ever never spoken about this doctor addressing a military officer as "Comrade Mrksic," have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, I did refer to this in my statement back in 1995. This is certainly not the first reference that I've made to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 1995 statement, you make no reference to a doctor who addressed an officer as "Comrade Mrksic." You told us in that statement in 1995 that you personally saw Mrksic, that he was there, and that he was giving orders, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrksic was speaking to that doctor. I'm not sure if it was Mrksic, in fact. He only called him "Mrksic" but I didn't know who Mrksic was. And this doctor was telling me about who each of the patients were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't say so in your 1995 statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did say that. I did say that I'd heard that, that the patients were being classified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please, to show the witness her own statement dated the 18th of July 1995? I will ask her to please read out a passage on page 4, passage 2 or paragraph 2 of the B/C/S. And on page 3, paragraph 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you please slowly read out the passage that I've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 20th of November at about 7.00 a.m., the slightly wounded and civilians were taken away from the hospital at the order of Major Sljivancanin and were boarded on to six buses. That morning, I saw a Serb doctor, it was either Dr. Stanojevic or Dr. Manojlovic, who are very much alike and I always confuse them. He was going around the corridor with a JNA officer pointing at the wounded saying, "This is one of ours, this is not one of ours." He was already wearing a military JNA uniform and no longer a white coat."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
